generation.hypothesis: Integrating reduced-order experimental microstructural descriptors (e.g., precipitate size distribution, volume fraction, interfacial area density) derived from the hierarchical heterostructure in HfNbTiVAl10 with a limited set of high-fidelity simulation results into a machine learning model will enable rapid and more accurate predictions of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior under tensile and fracture testing conditions compared to conventional atomistic or continuum simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy exhibiting a hierarchical heterostructure with multiple length‐scale features (nanoscale precipitates embedded in a matrix).
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a data-driven machine learning model that uses reduced-order microstructural descriptors alongside high-fidelity simulation inputs as training data.
generation.conditions: Tensile and fracture testing conducted under application-relevant strain rates and stress intensities, ensuring that the microstructural descriptors (from experimental characterization) accurately capture the features present in the alloy under quasi-static and dynamic loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Key microstructural descriptors such as precipitate size distribution, volume fraction, and interfacial area density that represent the hierarchical nature of the alloy’s microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The model learns the quantitative relationships between multi-scale structural features and macroscopic mechanical properties by combining experimental microstructural data with simulation-derived outputs. This hybrid approach reduces computational expense by avoiding full-scale simulations for every prediction while capturing critical heterogeneity effects that govern mechanical behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The machine learning model will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture characteristics with an improved accuracy (e.g., improved prediction error margins by a significant, but as-yet-uncertain percentage) and at a computational cost at least 20% lower than traditional simulation methods.
generation.baseline: Conventional simulation methods (atomistic/continuum models) that are either too computationally intensive or insufficiently accurate when accounting for the hierarchical heterogeneity in HfNbTiVAl10.
generation.boundary: The model may fail when the hierarchical microstructural features evolve significantly under extreme testing conditions, when the experimental descriptors cannot be accurately measured, or if the tested alloy compositions or processing conditions fall outside the range covered by the training dataset.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency are uncertain and dependent on the quality and representativeness of the experimental microstructural data used for training; furthermore, model generalizability to drastically different processing conditions remains to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Develop a machine learning model using a training dataset that combines experimentally obtained microstructural descriptors from HfNbTiVAl10 and a limited set of high-fidelity simulation results. Then, validate the model on a new batch of HfNbTiVAl10 samples subjected to tensile and fracture tests. Compare the mechanically measured properties with the model predictions and benchmark against conventional simulation methods.
measurements: Fracture behavior metrics (e.g., crack initiation and propagation rates)
Computational time required for prediction using the ML model versus traditional simulation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the machine learning model does not achieve at least a 20% reduction in computational time while also improving prediction accuracy (e.g., reducing prediction error by a significant margin relative to conventional methods) across multiple independent tests, or if the model fails to accurately predict the mechanical properties within the established error tolerance under the defined testing conditions, then the hypothesis is decisively falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In the present study, we employ a robust ML framework based primarily on Random Forest Regression (RFR) to predict the yield strength σYS and plastic strain εf of BCC and BCC+B2 HEAs. Our approach leverages physics-based features, including structural, elastic, electronic, and thermodynamic properties, to capture the intricate factors influencing mechanical properties. We curated a substantial dataset from established sources, focusing on compression data for their consistency and availability. Key features integral to our models include the D parameter γsfγusf, which is the ratio of the surface energy (γs) to the unstable stacking fault energy (γusf); the Variance of Mixing Enthalpy σΔHmix2, that quantifies the spread of heterogeneity in the interaction strengths among different atomic pairs in the alloys; and the ratio of testing temperature to melting temperature (TtestTmelt), representing the softening effect. We selected Random Forest Regression (RFR) as our primary ML algorithm due to its robustness against overfitting and its capability to handle high-dimensional data. Our use of a Genetic Algorithm (GA) for feature selection enhances the model’s performance by systematically evaluating and selecting the most relevant features. This approach improves predictive accuracy and provides insights into the physical significance of each feature, further validating our model’s interpretability. This interpretability is crucial for understanding the underlying mechanisms governing the mechanical properties of HEAs. The insights gained from our models can guide the design of new high-performance HEAs. By understanding the role of key features and their interactions, researchers can tailor alloy compositions to achieve desired mechanical properties, thus accelerating the discovery and optimization of advanced materials. Future work could explore the integration of additional physics-based features and the application of more advanced ensemble learning techniques. Expanding the dataset to include more diverse alloy compositions and testing conditions could further enhance the model’s robustness and applicability.

While many data-driven models have successfully predicted HEA phases using composition-based descriptors (e.g., average valence electron concentration, atomic size mismatch, and thermodynamic mixing quantities), here we pursue a complementary approach. We construct descriptors from DFT-derived pairwise interactions (such as binary formation enthalpies, volumes, and densities) to incorporate explicit information about atomic bonding and crystal structure preferences. The aim is to improve the interpretability of the model’s decisions by linking them to physical pair interactions, which could provide insights beyond what aggregate composition metrics offer. This DFT-based approach comes at a higher computational cost but offers a more direct connection to the underlying physics of phase stability. The objective of our study is to build a more interpretable model grounded in atomic-scale interactions. To achieve this, we utilize DFT-derived input features capturing pairwise bonding tendencies, in contrast to purely composition-driven descriptors used in past models. decision.trend: Early work in high‐entropy alloys focused on designing and characterizing hierarchical microstructures (e.g., intragranular nanoprecipitates and nano‐lamellar structures) to obtain record-high strengths and ductilities. Researchers first used conventional simulations (atomistic and continuum approaches) to rationalize these complex structures, but these methods quickly proved either too computationally expensive or insufficiently accurate in capturing multiple length-scale effects. Later studies began to incorporate more detailed experimental microstructural descriptors into interpretations as well as exploring atomic-level interactions. However, despite improvements in physical modeling, the ability to rapidly and accurately predict properties under realistic tensile and fracture conditions remained limited.
decision.unsolved: Existing simulation approaches do not adequately account for the hierarchical heterogeneity in alloys like HfNbTiVAl10, leading to either extended computational times or accuracy deficits. There is a pressing need for an approach that harnesses data from experimentally resolved microstructure features to yield fast, quantitative predictions of elastic modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior that also clearly delineates conditions where the model may no longer hold.
decision.lever: Develop a machine learning model that integrates reduced-order microstructural descriptors (e.g., precipitate size distribution, volume fraction, interfacial area density of hierarchical features) with a small set of high-fidelity simulation results to predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related metrics under tensile/fracture conditions. Key parameters would include descriptor selection (which capture the hierarchical length scales), training on multi-scale experimental data paired with simulations, and validation against independent tensile testing.
decision.why: The trend shows a shift from purely physics-based and exhaustive simulation techniques to approaches that leverage detailed microstructural information to bridge scale differences. Given that established simulations struggle with computational cost and accuracy for hierarchical systems, a data-driven solution that harnesses experimental descriptors is the next logical advance. This lever directly addresses the constraint of rapid and reliable predictions and builds upon earlier work that demonstrated the importance of hierarchical features in governing mechanical properties.
